conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my role is to listen and help you feel supported as you navigate new motherhood. Over the next few minutes we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally during the past week. This is a routine screening that looks at mood, anxiety, and coping; it helps us figure out what kind of support or resources might be most helpful for you right now.  

Everything we discuss is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are ten short questions, and we’ll go at your pace. If any question feels difficult, we can pause or come back to it. When you’re ready, we’ll begin with the first one.

In the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?
Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not as often as before the baby, but when my husband makes a silly joke or when I see the baby’s funny faces, I do laugh. It doesn’t feel forced or anything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most of the time, yes—I can still laugh. It might take a little more effort if I’m tired, but funny moments still get me smiling.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yeah, I still look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee once the baby’s down for a nap, or taking her out in the stroller when the weather’s nice. They’re small things, but they feel good.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. If she spits up right after I’ve changed her or I can’t figure out why she’s fussy, I might think “ugh, what did I miss?” for a second, but I don’t stay stuck on it. I figure we’re both learning.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do get little waves of worry—like wondering if her breathing sounds normal or if she’s eating enough—but they pass quickly and I can usually settle myself. It doesn’t feel totally out of the blue, more like normal new-mom checking.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that kind of sudden fear or panic. I might feel a little on edge when she cries and I can’t soothe her right away, but it’s not a “heart racing, can’t breathe” thing.
Things have been getting on top of me
Sometimes, yeah—like yesterday when she wouldn’t nap and the laundry was piling up, I felt a bit swamped. It passes once I tick one thing off the list or my partner steps in.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s actually been okay—when I get the chance to sleep, I fall asleep pretty easily. I’m more tired from being up with her than from lying awake feeling upset.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I have the normal tired or overwhelmed moments, but I wouldn’t call them sad or miserable—more like “this is hard today,” and then it lifts.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried at all this week. I might feel a bit teary if I’m really tired, but it hasn’t actually happened.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Screening note – Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) responses reviewed:

Symptoms endorsed:
- Occasional “waves of worry” about infant (Q4) and situational feeling of being “swamped” when tasks accumulate (Q6).
- Denies persistent low mood, loss of pleasure, tearfulness, sleep-onset problems related to mood, inappropriate guilt, panic, or self-harm thoughts (Q1-3, 5, 7-10).

Pattern:
- Maintains ability to laugh and anticipate enjoyment; worry is context-specific to infant care and resolves quickly. No evidence of pervasive depressive or anxiety symptoms.

Risk screening:
- No current indicators for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder; no safety concerns identified.
